title: Sandisk Stock: Buy, Sell, or Hold?
detail:
Sandisk Stock: Buy, Sell, or Hold?
Marc Guberti, The Motley Fool

NVDA
005930.KS
MSFT
GOOG

Trading disclosure

Sandisk (NASDAQ: SNDK) stock has more than quintupled year to date, but despite those gains, its rally still doesn't appear to be over. The long-term tailwinds in the memory market just accelerated, and Sandisk is one of the best-positioned companies in the industry.

Image source: Getty Images.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Recent Samsung news will trickle to Sandisk's bottom line

Investors have greatly underestimated the durability of the current memory chip boom, even the most bullish ones. Samsung (OTC: SSNLF) recently reported that three large customers had signed deals locking up 70% of its memory chip capacity through 2031: Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA), Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT), and Alphabet (NASDAQ: GOOG) (NASDAQ: GOOGL).

Those deals are a big catalyst for the entire memory sector, and while Samsung is the immediate beneficiary, Sandisk may emerge as the bigger winner. That's because Sandisk has been growing sales at a faster rate than Samsung, thanks to its NAND flash memory storage chips.

Samsung reported 130% year-over-year revenue growth in the second quarter, while Sandisk delivered 372% year-over-year revenue growth. Sandisk told investors in its 2026 Investor Day that it, too, is securing multiyear deals with its top customers. The Samsung news has further limited the volume of memory chips that will be available for future customers, which will make it easier for Sandisk to command higher prices and sign more attractive multiyear deals.

These developments continue to squash the narrative about the cyclicality of the memory chip industry. While boom-and-bust cycles have long been the norm, these multiyear deals offer clear revenue visibility and demand, and lock in price floors. AI-driven demand for memory is also unlikely to slow down as companies invest more heavily in physical AI platforms such as humanoid robots and self-driving vehicles.

Sandisk stock remains cheap thanks to impressive growth rates

It's not every day that a growth stock can more than quintuple in eight months while having fundamentals that justify that move, but Sandisk's fundamentals do. The company went from a net loss in its fiscal 2025 fourth quarter to $6.9 billion in net income during its fiscal 2026 fourth quarter. This resulted in a compelling 77% net profit margin for the recent period.

title: Is Oracle Stock A Hedge Or A Downside Trap?
detail:
Is Oracle Stock A Hedge Or A Downside Trap?
Trefis Team

IBM
GOOG
MSFT
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Photo by Dx21 on Pixabay

The tech giant's sudden swings can be disorienting, but its true significance for your portfolio lies in its distinct, high-octane behavior.

Oracle (ORCL) has been a study in sharp swings lately, giving back a recent multi-day climb with a 5% drop yesterday even as the broader index held steady. The volatile stretch has coincided with a steady cadence of announcements, from expanding its AI agent capabilities in healthcare to earning top marks for its supply chain management suites.

That kind of whiplash triggers a familiar investor instinct: the urge to time the bottom or guess where the next leg heads.

For disciplined portfolio management, the central question isn't where Oracle stock heads next week, but how its volatility alters your total risk exposure. How much of its return is genuinely its own story, and how much is just a reflection of the market you likely already own through an index fund?

A Return Stream With Its Own Rules

According to our quantitative trailing five-year analysis, Oracle's stock has moved with a 0.48 correlation to the S&P 500. That number tells a compelling story. A reading of 1.0 would mean it's a perfect copy of the market; a 0 would mean it's completely independent. At 0.48, Oracle lives in a valuable middle ground: it shares some of the market's general direction but keeps a substantial amount of its behavior for itself. For an investor seeking growth, this profile cuts both ways. You aren't just buying conventional market risk; you are taking on a volatile, idiosyncratic driver that decouples from the broader index.

The $70 Billion Price of Powering AI

That independent streak is grounded in a high-stakes business transformation aimed at powering an AI Boom. Oracle is in the midst of a large-scale build-out to meet substantial demand for its cloud and AI infrastructure. The company's backlog of remaining performance obligations, or RPO, has swelled to $638 billion. On its latest earnings call, management reported signing $67 billion in AI infrastructure contracts in a single quarter.

This is the engine driving Oracle's unique story, but the bill for Oracle's AI build-out is steep. The company plans a net cash outlay for capital expenditures of around $70 billion in fiscal 2027 and expects to raise around $40 billion in debt and equity to help fund it. Management has been clear that this spending will pressure gross margins in the near term.

How Oracle Amplifies Your Portfolio

So, what role does Oracle play in a portfolio? It's a high-octane source of differentiated volatility, not a shock absorber. Its behavior over the past year makes this clear. On days the S&P 500 rose, Oracle captured about 197% of the market's gain. But on days the market fell, it absorbed about 307% of the loss. It tends to fall harder than it rises, relative to the market.

title: How Wide Is the Range of Possibilities for Adobe Stock?
detail:
How Wide Is the Range of Possibilities for Adobe Stock?
Trefis Team
Wed, September 2, 2026 at 10:42 AM PDT 4 min read
ORCL-PD
MSFT
ADSK
ADBE
GOOG
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Image by StockSnap from Pixabay

The options market is pricing a sizable year-long swing for the software giant, and if you hold the shares, you are already exposed to the full ride.

If you own shares of Adobe (ADBE), you might think of it as a stable pillar of the software world. But the market that prices risk for a living, the options market, is telling a very different story about the year ahead. It's pricing a level of uncertainty that implies a wide range of outcomes, and as a shareholder, you're carrying that risk whether you trade options or not.

A Priced Range from $180 to $471

Let's put some numbers on it. From its current price of about $292.79, the options market is pricing a 68% probability that Adobe stock will finish the next year somewhere between a floor near $180 and a ceiling near $470.95. That's a potential drop of 39% on the low end or a climb of 61% on the high end. This isn't a forecast; it's a price tag on uncertainty. The key takeaway is the sheer size of that potential swing. If you own the stock, you own that entire two-sided risk.

Why the Market Is Pricing More Risk Than Usual

This isn't just business as usual. The market's priced-in volatility of 46% is running at 1.18 times the stock's actual, historical volatility of 40%. That premium, along with broad implied volatility in the 78th percentile of its annual range, tells you traders are bracing for a bigger move.

A Strategic Pivot Meets A Leadership Transition

What's driving this uncertainty? Adobe is in the middle of a significant strategic pivot. The company is aggressively shifting to a freemium model for products like Firefly and Express to capture new users, and the early numbers are sizable: management noted on its latest call that "Creative Freemium MAU" grew "from 50 million to 90 million year over year." The bull case is that this user acquisition will eventually convert into long-term growth.

But this pivot comes at a cost. Management also stated the shift "lowers our second half ARR growth expectations" and that they decided to "defer previously planned Creative Cloud second half line optimizations." The payback on this strategy, they suggest, will "play out, I think, over 2027." Compounding this uncertainty is a major leadership transition, with the company navigating both a "CEO search" and the departure of its CFO. This combination of a long-term strategic initiative against a near-term financial headwind, all during a leadership change, is exactly what creates such a wide range of potential outcomes. As a brief side note, traders are currently paying about 1.8 times as much for upside speculation as for downside protection, suggesting a tilt of interest toward the bull case playing out.

A CNBC segment on September 1, 2026 flagged something odd in Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) options activity. A single participant unwound two long-dated bullish call spreads for a combined credit of roughly $36 million, and the contracts still had over a year left to run before their December 2027 expiry.

That single trade is probably not a signal on its own. One trader closing one position is one decision by one participant with unknown motives, and the range of plausible reasons runs from a fund rebalancing to a risk manager cutting exposure to a considered call that Microsoft will not clear the higher strikes by then.

What is worth doing is putting the flow next to what Microsoft actually reported in July and asking whether the stock's flat stretch this year is a pause or a repricing. The shares closed at $501.02 on Tuesday, up 8.02% over the past month but essentially flat over the past year at -0.3%.

What the Options Print Actually Tells You

CNBC's Oliver Renick described the trade this way: "Someone closed out two bullish call spreads a 595 to 705 spread worth 19 million and a 610 to 725 worth about 17 million. The trades spanned more than 30,000 call contracts, for a total credit of about 36 million."

The AI Engine That Re-Accelerated Snowflake

Photo by wynpnt on Pixabay

You watched the stock nearly double in six months. The reason was a new class of AI tools that just turned into a powerful growth accelerant.

If you held Snowflake (SNOW) stock over the last six months, you had a good run. A very good run. From early March to the end of August, the shares climbed 88%, leaving the S&P 500's 11% return in the dust. It even blew past cloud giant Microsoft, which gained 26% over the same period. So what exactly happened to justify that kind of performance?

What Flipped The Switch? A 34% Growth Re-Acceleration.

The story changed on May 27. That's when the company reported its first-quarter results and revealed a crucial shift in its trajectory. Product revenue growth accelerated to 34% year-over-year. That figure was up from 30% the prior quarter and 26% a year ago. For a company of this scale, continued growth is one thing; accelerating growth is what truly gets the market's attention. It was, in management's words, the company's "strongest sequential dollar growth in company history."

And Where Did That New Growth Come From? Cortex Code.

The acceleration wasn't a fluke. It was driven by a new suite of artificial intelligence products, particularly a tool for developers called Cortex Code, or CoCo. Management noted that these new AI tools are seeing the "fastest adoption of any new products in our history." This created a powerful flywheel effect: AI is driving more usage of the core data platform while also becoming a significant new revenue stream on its own. The company's confidence was so high that it raised its full-year growth outlook from 27% to 31%, signaling that this new momentum has legs.

But Are These AI Products Actually As Profitable?

Here is where the picture gets more complicated. These new AI tools are a hit with customers, but they come with a different cost structure. The company's finance chief confirmed that its "AI products have a lower gross margin than our core platform." While management says it is finding other efficiencies to maintain its 75% product gross margin target for the year, it introduces a new variable for investors. The very engine driving this impressive new growth is less profitable than the core business. We have explored how this dynamic might affect the stock's future prospects. The market has clearly embraced the growth story for now, but it leaves one critical question unanswered.

With customers now paying by the query for a powerful new AI tool, how long until they start watching the meter?

title: What's the Real Fuel for Apple Stock's Next Climb?
detail:
What's the Real Fuel for Apple Stock's Next Climb?
Trefis Team
Wed, September 2, 2026 at 9:34 AM PDT 4 min read
AAPL
AMZN
SWKS
HPQ
DELL
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Photo by geralt on Pixabay

The biggest opportunity for the stock isn't some futuristic gadget, but a powerful dynamic hiding in plain sight in its latest results.

Apple (AAPL) stock has delivered a handsome 40% return over the past year, and with the business firing on all cylinders, you might be asking a fair question: what on earth could drive it materially higher from here?

The answer isn't a secret new product or a far-off technological breakthrough. It's something much more immediate. The single biggest opportunity for Apple is simply its ability to catch up to the substantial, record-setting demand it's already seeing for its core products.

A 'Remarkably Better' Problem to Have

Apple's engine is running hot. In its most recent quarter, the company posted a record $109.4 billion in revenue, up 16% from a year ago. The growth in its core products was even more impressive. iPhone revenue surged 22% to $54.3 billion, while the Mac division put up its best June quarter ever, growing an eye-watering 29% to $10.4 billion. Management was candid about the situation, calling it a demand forecast issue. where the iPhone and the Mac are both doing remarkably better than we thought they would do.

The results go beyond a single good quarter, signaling an overwhelming consumer appetite, fueled by excitement around new features like Siri AI, which management is "off the charts excited about." This raises the question of just how much upside this growth can deliver.

What's Holding It Back?

Here's the tension in the story. That incredible demand is running headlong into a wall of supply constraints. The company has "less flexibility in the supply chain than normal," and the problem is getting worse, not better. Management stated plainly that it expects "the impact from the supply constraints to increase significantly sequentially" in the upcoming September quarter, affecting iPhone, Mac, and iPad. This is the primary reason the company's rapid growth is guided to a slower pace of 9%-11% for the period.

In short, Apple can't make its most popular products fast enough to meet the current wave of demand. It's a fantastic problem to have, but it's a problem nonetheless, and it's capping the company's true potential right now.

Unlocking the Backlog

This is where the forward-looking opportunity comes into focus. The upside from here isn't about inventing a new category; it's about unlocking the revenue currently trapped behind that supply bottleneck. As Apple works to resolve these constraints over the coming quarters, it can begin to satisfy that pent-up demand. Every step it takes to close the gap between what it can build and what the world wants to buy represents a potential tailwind for revenue.
